en: I usually wake up at six on weekdays.
tamil: நான் பொதுவா வார நாட்கள்ல ஆறு மணிக்கு எழுந்திருப்பேன்.
context: Describing your morning habit.
explain: Present simple with 'usually' talks about habits and routines.
usage: Use it when friends or colleagues ask about your daily routine.
leelaQ: What time do you usually wake up on weekdays?
answer: I usually wake up at six, then I make tea.

en: She is cooking dinner right now.
context: Telling a caller why your mother cannot talk.
explain: Present continuous (is + verb-ing) is for actions happening at this moment.
usage: Use it on the phone when someone asks where a family member is.
leelaQ: What is your mother doing right now?
answer: She is watching TV in the hall right now.

en: We went to Madurai last Sunday.
context: Telling a colleague about your weekend.
explain: Past simple with 'last Sunday' talks about a finished time in the past.
usage: Use it on Monday morning when colleagues ask about your weekend.
leelaQ: Where did you go last weekend?
answer: I went to my grandmother's house last weekend.

en: I will call you after the meeting.
tamil: மீட்டிங் முடிஞ்சதுக்கப்புறம் நான் உங்களுக்கு கால் பண்றேன்.
context: Promising to call a client back.
explain: 'Will' + verb is used for promises and quick decisions about the future.
usage: Use it with a client or friend when you cannot talk right now.
leelaQ: Will you call your friend after work today?
answer: Yes, I will call him after work today.

en: I have already finished the report.
context: Telling your manager the work is done.
explain: Present perfect (have + past participle) with 'already' shows something is done before now.
usage: Use it when your manager asks about the status of a task.
leelaQ: Have you finished your work for today?
answer: Yes, I have already finished everything.

en: You should drink more water in this heat.
tamil: இந்த வெயில்ல நீ இன்னும் அதிகமா தண்ணி குடிக்கணும்.
context: Giving advice to a friend in summer.
explain: 'Should' + verb gives friendly advice.
usage: Use it to advise a friend or family member kindly.
leelaQ: What should people do in hot weather?
answer: People should drink water and stay in the shade.

en: Please close the window before you leave.
context: Asking a coworker to close up the office.
explain: An imperative with 'please' is a polite instruction or request.
usage: Use it with a colleague or helper at the end of the day.
leelaQ: What do you check before you leave home?
answer: I check the gas, the lights, and the windows.

en: If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.
tamil: நாளைக்கு மழை பெஞ்சா நாங்க பிக்னிக்கை ரத்து பண்ணிடுவோம்.
context: Planning an outing with friends.
explain: First conditional: if + present simple, then will + verb for a real possibility.
usage: Use it when making plans that depend on the weather.
leelaQ: What will you do if it rains this weekend?
answer: If it rains, I will stay at home and read.

en: If I had more time, I would learn the guitar.
tamil: எனக்கு இன்னும் நேரம் இருந்தா நான் கிட்டார் கத்துக்குவேன்.
context: Talking about a hobby you wish you could start.
explain: Second conditional: if + past simple, would + verb for an unreal or unlikely situation.
usage: Use it to talk about dreams or wishes in a casual chat.
leelaQ: What would you learn if you had more free time?
answer: If I had more time, I would learn to swim.

en: The bill was paid by my brother.
context: Explaining who paid at a restaurant.
explain: Passive voice (was + past participle) puts the focus on the action, not the doer.
usage: Use it when you want to say what happened without stressing who did it.
leelaQ: Who paid the bill the last time you ate out?
answer: The bill was paid by my friend last time.

en: Our new office will be opened next month.
tamil: எங்க புது ஆபீஸ் அடுத்த மாசம் திறக்கப்படும்.
context: Sharing company news with a friend.
explain: Future passive (will be + past participle) is used for planned events.
usage: Use it to share announcements about plans or events.
leelaQ: What will be built near your house soon?
answer: A new metro station will be built near my house soon.

en: Chennai is hotter than Bengaluru.
context: Comparing two cities with a friend.
explain: Comparative adjective + 'than' compares two things.
usage: Use it when you compare places, prices or people in conversation.
leelaQ: Which is hotter, your city or Chennai?
answer: My city is cooler than Chennai.

en: Is this phone as good as that one?
tamil: இந்த போன் அதே மாதிரி நல்லா இருக்குமா?
context: Asking a shopkeeper to compare two phones.
explain: 'As ... as' compares two things that are equal.
usage: Use it while shopping when two items look similar.
leelaQ: Which is better for you, a phone or a laptop?
answer: A laptop is as useful as a phone, but I carry my phone more.

en: He is the tallest boy in the class.
context: Describing a classmate to a new teacher.
explain: 'The tallest' is a superlative for one-syllable adjectives; add -est.
usage: Use it to point out one person from a group.
leelaQ: Who is the tallest person in your family?
answer: My uncle is the tallest person in my family.

en: Could you please send me an email?
tamil: தயவு செய்து எனக்கு ஒரு மெயில் அனுப்ப முடியுமா?
context: Asking a colleague to share details in writing.
explain: 'Could you please' is a very polite way to ask for something.
usage: Use it with seniors or clients when you want things in writing.
leelaQ: How do you ask a colleague to send a file?
answer: I say, could you please send me the file?

en: May I come in, sir?
context: Asking permission to enter your manager's room.
explain: 'May I' is a formal way to ask for permission.
usage: Use it at the door of a manager, teacher or interviewer.
leelaQ: What do you say before entering a teacher's room?
answer: I say, may I come in, sir?

en: You must wear a helmet while riding a bike.
context: Reminding a younger cousin about road safety.
explain: 'Must' shows a strong rule or duty.
usage: Use it to explain rules or important safety advice.
leelaQ: What must people do for road safety?
answer: People must follow the signals and wear helmets.

en: You don't have to wait for me.
context: Telling a friend to go ahead without you.
explain: 'Don't have to' means it is not necessary, but you are free to do it.
usage: Use it kindly when you do not want to delay someone.
leelaQ: What do you say if you will be late and a friend is waiting?
answer: I say, you don't have to wait for me.

en: She can speak three languages.
context: Praising a friend's skills.
explain: 'Can' shows ability.
usage: Use it to talk about what someone is able to do.
leelaQ: How many languages can you speak?
answer: I can speak Tamil, English and a little Hindi.

en: I couldn't open the file you sent.
tamil: நீங்க அனுப்பின ஃபைலை என்னால திறக்க முடியல.
context: Telling a coworker about a technical problem.
explain: 'Couldn't' is the past of 'can't' and shows you were not able to do something.
usage: Use it when you face a problem with something someone sent.
leelaQ: What do you say if an email attachment does not open?
answer: I say, I couldn't open the file, please send it again.

en: This is the book that I told you about.
tamil: இது தான் நான் உன்கிட்ட சொன்ன புத்தகம்.
context: Showing a friend a book you recommended.
explain: 'That' links the noun 'book' to extra information in a relative clause.
usage: Use it when you show or give someone something you mentioned earlier.
leelaQ: Which book did you tell your friends about?
answer: I told them about a book on healthy habits.

en: The shop where I bought this phone is closed today.
tamil: நான் இந்த போன் வாங்கின கடை இன்னைக்கு மூடியிருக்கு.
context: Explaining why you cannot return a phone.
explain: 'Where' begins a relative clause that describes a place.
usage: Use it when you need to explain which place you mean.
leelaQ: Where do you usually buy your groceries?
answer: I buy them at the shop where my mother always goes.

en: She works as a nurse in a government hospital.
tamil: அவங்க ஒரு அரசு மருத்துவமனையில நர்ஸா வேலை பாக்குறாங்க.
context: Telling someone about your sister's job.
explain: 'A' is used before a singular job or noun; 'as' shows the role.
usage: Use it when you talk about someone's work.
leelaQ: What does your sister or brother do for work?
answer: My brother works as an engineer in a small company.

en: I'll meet you at the bus stop at five.
tamil: நான் அஞ்சு மணிக்கு பஸ் ஸ்டாப்புல உன்ன பாக்கறேன்.
context: Fixing a time and place with a friend.
explain: 'At' is used for exact times and points; 'will' for a decision.
usage: Use it when you fix a meeting with a friend.
leelaQ: Where will you meet your friends this weekend?
answer: I will meet them at the mall at four.

en: My birthday is on the tenth of December.
context: Telling a colleague your birthday date.
explain: Use 'on' with dates and days, 'in' with months, 'at' with times.
usage: Use it when someone asks for your date of birth or birthday.
leelaQ: When is your birthday?
answer: My birthday is on the fifth of March.

en: He has been working here since 2019.
tamil: அவர் 2019 ல இருந்து இங்க வேலை பாக்குறார்.
context: Introducing a senior colleague to a new joiner.
explain: Present perfect continuous with 'since' shows an action that began in the past and continues now.
usage: Use it to say how long you have been doing something.
leelaQ: How long have you been living in your city?
answer: I have been living here for ten years.

en: Have you ever eaten Kerala parotta?
context: Asking a friend about food experiences.
explain: 'Have you ever ...?' asks about experiences at any time in life.
usage: Use it to start a friendly talk about food or travel.
leelaQ: Have you ever travelled by flight?
answer: Yes, I have travelled by flight twice.

en: She hasn't replied to my message yet.
tamil: அவங்க என் மெசேஜுக்கு இன்னும் பதில் சொல்லல.
context: Complaining mildly about a slow reply.
explain: Present perfect negative with 'yet' shows something expected has not happened up to now.
usage: Use it when you wait for an answer and talk about it with a friend.
leelaQ: What do you do when someone has not replied to your message?
answer: I wait for some time and then I call them.

en: When I reached the station, the train had already left.
tamil: நான் ஸ்டேஷனுக்கு போனப்போ ரயில் ஏற்கனவே போயிடுச்சு.
context: Telling a friend why you missed your train.
explain: Past perfect (had + past participle) shows an earlier action before another past action.
usage: Use it to explain what happened first in a story.
leelaQ: Have you ever missed a bus or train? What happened?
answer: Yes, when I reached the stop, the bus had already left.

en: While I was cooking, the power went off.
context: Telling a friend about a small problem at home.
explain: Past continuous (was + verb-ing) shows an action in progress when another action interrupted it.
usage: Use it to tell a story about something that interrupted you.
leelaQ: What were you doing when the power last went off?
answer: I was watching TV when the power went off.

en: I'm going to start yoga from Monday.
tamil: நான் திங்கள்கிழமையில இருந்து யோகா ஆரம்பிக்கப் போறேன்.
context: Sharing a new plan with a friend.
explain: 'Going to' + verb shows a plan or intention you have already decided.
usage: Use it to share a plan you have made.
leelaQ: What are you going to start soon?
answer: I am going to start walking every morning.

en: Are they coming to the wedding?
context: Asking a cousin about guests.
explain: Present continuous questions: am/is/are + subject + verb-ing.
usage: Use it when you plan an event and want to know who will attend.
leelaQ: Who is coming to your next family function?
answer: My cousins and uncles are coming.

en: It's getting dark, so let's go home.
context: Suggesting to leave to a friend in the evening.
explain: Present continuous with 'get' shows a change that is happening slowly.
usage: Use it when a situation is changing and you suggest an action.
leelaQ: What do you do when it is getting dark outside?
answer: I switch on the lights and close the windows.

en: Let's have tea before we start.
context: Suggesting a short break before work.
explain: 'Let's' + verb makes a friendly suggestion for both of you.
usage: Use it with friends or teammates to suggest something together.
leelaQ: What do you suggest to your friends when you are tired?
answer: Let's take a short walk and have some tea.

en: Turn left at the temple and go straight.
context: Giving directions to a stranger.
explain: Imperatives are used to give directions and instructions.
usage: Use it when someone asks you the way.
leelaQ: How do you give directions to your house?
answer: Turn right at the signal and go straight for two minutes.

en: Don't forget to take your medicine.
context: Reminding an elderly parent.
explain: 'Don't' + verb is a negative imperative; it warns or reminds.
usage: Use it with family members to remind them kindly.
leelaQ: What do you remind your parents about every day?
answer: I remind them to take their tablets and drink water.

en: Never touch electric wires with wet hands.
context: Warning a child about safety.
explain: 'Never' + verb is a strong negative imperative for warnings.
usage: Use it to warn children or new helpers about danger.
leelaQ: What safety rules do you teach children at home?
answer: I tell them never to play near the stove.

en: Please be quiet, the baby is sleeping.
tamil: தயவு செய்து அமைதியா இருங்க, குழந்தை தூங்குது.
context: Asking guests to lower their voice.
explain: Use 'please' with an imperative to be polite.
usage: Use it at home when someone is speaking too loudly.
leelaQ: What do you say if the room is too noisy?
answer: I say, please be quiet, I am studying.

en: Would you like some more rice?
context: Serving a guest at home.
explain: 'Would you like' is a polite offer.
usage: Use it when you host guests and offer food.
leelaQ: What do you say when you serve guests at home?
answer: I say, would you like some more rice?

en: Shall I carry your bag for you?
context: Offering help to an elderly woman.
explain: 'Shall I' offers to do something for another person.
usage: Use it to offer help to someone who is carrying a load.
leelaQ: How do you offer help to an elderly person?
answer: I say, shall I carry your bag for you?

en: I would rather stay at home today.
context: Declining an outing politely.
explain: 'Would rather' + verb shows what you prefer.
usage: Use it to say what you prefer without sounding rude.
leelaQ: Would you rather stay home or go out on holidays?
answer: I would rather go out and meet my friends.

en: You might want to check the schedule again.
context: Giving a soft suggestion to a coworker.
explain: 'Might want to' is a gentle, polite way to give advice.
usage: Use it with colleagues when you point out a possible mistake.
leelaQ: How do you politely tell someone to check their work?
answer: I say, you might want to check this once more.

en: It may rain this evening, so take a jacket.
tamil: இன்னைக்கு சாயங்காலம் மழை வரலாம், அதனால ஜாக்கெட் எடுத்துக்கோ.
context: Advising a friend before going out.
explain: 'May' shows a possibility, not a sure thing.
usage: Use it when you give weather advice to a friend or family member.
leelaQ: What do you take with you when it may rain?
answer: I take an umbrella and a small towel.

en: He must be tired after the long journey.
tamil: நீண்ட பயணத்துக்கு அப்புறம் அவன் களைப்பா இருப்பான்.
context: Guessing about your uncle's condition.
explain: 'Must be' is used when you are almost sure something is true.
usage: Use it when you guess something based on what you see or know.
leelaQ: How do you feel after a long journey?
answer: I must be very tired, so I sleep early.

en: Can you tell me what time the bank opens?
tamil: வங்கி எத்தனை மணிக்கு திறப்பாங்கனு சொல்ல முடியுமா?
context: Calling a bank for information.
explain: Indirect questions with 'Can you tell me' use statement word order after the question word.
usage: Use it on the phone or at an enquiry counter.
leelaQ: What do you ask when you call a bank?
answer: I ask what time the bank opens.

en: I'm not sure whether he will come.
context: Answering about an uncertain guest.
explain: 'Whether' introduces a doubt or a choice between two possibilities.
usage: Use it when you are not certain about someone's plan.
leelaQ: Are you sure about your plans for next weekend?
answer: I am not sure whether I will go out.

en: She told me that she would be late.
tamil: தான் தாமதமா வருவேன்னு அவ என்கிட்ட சொன்னா.
context: Reporting what a friend said.
explain: Reported speech moves the verb one step back: 'will' becomes 'would'.
usage: Use it when you tell someone what another person said.
leelaQ: What did your friend tell you the last time you met?
answer: She told me that she was starting a new job.

en: He asked me if I wanted some coffee.
context: Repeating a question to a friend.
explain: In reported questions, use 'if' or 'whether' and no question word order.
usage: Use it when you tell someone what a person asked you.
leelaQ: What did your colleague ask you today?
answer: He asked me if I had finished the report.

en: I'm used to waking up early.
context: Talking about a habit with a roommate.
explain: 'Be used to' + verb-ing means something is normal for you now.
usage: Use it when you explain what is normal and easy for you.
leelaQ: What are you used to doing every day?
answer: I am used to walking to work every day.

en: We used to play cricket in the street.
context: Remembering your childhood with a friend.
explain: 'Used to' + verb talks about past habits that no longer happen.
usage: Use it when you remember how life was earlier.
leelaQ: What did you use to play as a child?
answer: I used to play kabaddi with my neighbours.

en: I forgot to bring my ID card today.
tamil: நான் இன்னைக்கு ஐடி கார்டு கொண்டு வர மறந்துட்டேன்.
context: Telling the security guard at the office gate.
explain: 'Forgot to' + verb means you did not do something you should have done.
usage: Use it politely at an office or college gate.
leelaQ: What did you forget to bring recently?
answer: I forgot to bring my lunch box.

en: Thank you for helping me with this.
context: Thanking a teammate after finishing a task.
explain: 'Thank you for' is followed by verb-ing.
usage: Use it at work or home to show you appreciate someone's help.
leelaQ: Who helped you recently, and how do you thank them?
answer: My friend helped me move, and I thanked him with lunch.

en: I'm looking forward to meeting your family.
context: Saying something warm to a future in-law.
explain: 'Look forward to' is followed by verb-ing, not a base verb.
usage: Use it to show you are happy about a coming event.
leelaQ: What are you looking forward to this month?
answer: I am looking forward to my sister's wedding.

en: Sorry, I'm late because the bus broke down.
tamil: மன்னிக்கணும், பஸ் ரிப்பேர் ஆயிடுச்சு, அதான் தாமதம்.
context: Apologising to your manager for being late.
explain: 'Because' gives a reason; 'broke down' is a phrasal verb in past simple.
usage: Use it when you apologise and explain a delay.
leelaQ: What do you say when you reach late?
answer: I say sorry and tell the reason for being late.

en: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
tamil: மழை பெய்துட்டு இருந்தாலும் நாங்க வாக்கிங் போனோம்.
context: Telling a friend about a rainy evening.
explain: 'Although' joins two opposite ideas in one sentence.
usage: Use it when you tell a story with a surprise or contrast.
leelaQ: What did you do even though the weather was bad?
answer: Although it was cold, I went out for tea.

en: I was tired, but I finished my work anyway.
tamil: நான் களைப்பா இருந்தேன், ஆனாலும் என் வேலையை முடிச்சேன்.
context: Telling your manager you completed the task.
explain: 'But' joins two ideas that contrast; 'anyway' means in spite of that.
usage: Use it to show you stayed committed to a task.
leelaQ: When did you finish something even though you were tired?
answer: I finished my project late at night, but I was happy.

en: Neither of my parents drinks coffee.
tamil: என் அப்பா அம்மா ரெண்டு பேருமே காபி குடிக்க மாட்டாங்க.
context: Chatting about family habits.
explain: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb and has a negative meaning.
usage: Use it when something is true for none of two people.
leelaQ: Do both your parents drink coffee or tea?
answer: My mother drinks tea, but my father drinks coffee.

en: There isn't any sugar left in the kitchen.
context: Telling your mother before shopping.
explain: 'Isn't any' is used with uncountable nouns in negative sentences.
usage: Use it at home before you make a shopping list.
leelaQ: What is finished in your kitchen right now?
answer: There is no milk left in the kitchen.

en: How much rice do we need for ten people?
tamil: பத்து பேருக்கு நமக்கு எவ்வளவு அரிசி வேணும்?
context: Planning food for a function.
explain: 'How much' is used with uncountable nouns such as rice.
usage: Use it when you plan food or shopping for a group.
leelaQ: How much tea do you drink every day?
answer: I drink about three cups of tea every day.

en: How many chairs are there in the hall?
context: Setting up for a meeting.
explain: 'How many' is used with countable nouns such as chairs.
usage: Use it when you count things before an event.
leelaQ: How many people live in your house?
answer: Five people live in my house.

en: There are a few mangoes in the basket.
context: Telling your sister what is available.
explain: 'A few' is used with countable nouns and means a small number.
usage: Use it to tell someone how much of something is available.
leelaQ: What do you have a few of at home?
answer: I have a few books on my table.

en: I have little time today, so please be quick.
tamil: எனக்கு இன்னைக்கு நேரம் ரொம்ப கம்மி, அதனால சீக்கிரம் பண்ணுங்க.
context: Asking a service person to be quick.
explain: 'Little' (without 'a') means almost none and is used with uncountable nouns.
usage: Use it when you are in a hurry and need to be polite.
leelaQ: What do you do when you have very little time?
answer: I make a list and finish the important work first.

en: The meeting has been postponed until Friday.
context: Updating a team about a change.
explain: Present perfect passive (has been + past participle) tells a result that matters now.
usage: Use it when you announce a change of plans at work.
leelaQ: What was recently postponed in your life?
answer: My trip was postponed until next month.

en: My phone was stolen in the bus yesterday.
tamil: என் போன் நேத்து பஸ்ல திருடு போயிடுச்சு.
context: Reporting a theft at a police station.
explain: Past passive (was + past participle) is used when the doer is unknown.
usage: Use it when you report a problem and do not know who did it.
leelaQ: What do you do if your phone is stolen?
answer: I report it to the police and block my SIM.

en: Was this food prepared without onion?
context: Asking at a restaurant during a fasting day.
explain: Passive questions put 'was/were' before the subject.
usage: Use it at a restaurant when you have a food restriction.
leelaQ: How do you ask about the ingredients in a dish?
answer: I ask, is this prepared without garlic?

en: I'd like to book a table for four, please.
tamil: நாலு பேருக்கு ஒரு டேபிள் புக் பண்ணணும்.
context: Calling a restaurant to reserve a table.
explain: 'I'd like to' is a polite way to say what you want.
usage: Use it on the phone when you make a booking.
leelaQ: What do you say when you book a table?
answer: I say, I'd like to book a table for four, please.

en: Why don't we take a taxi instead?
context: Making a suggestion to a friend when you are late.
explain: 'Why don't we' is a friendly way to make a suggestion.
usage: Use it with friends or family when you suggest a better plan.
leelaQ: What do you suggest when it rains heavily?
answer: Why don't we stay at home and watch a movie?

en: How about trying the new restaurant on Anna Nagar road?
tamil: அண்ணா நகர் ரோட்டுல இருக்குற புது ஹோட்டலுக்கு போய் பாக்கலாமா?
context: Suggesting a lunch place to colleagues.
explain: 'How about' + verb-ing is a casual way to suggest something.
usage: Use it to suggest food, plans or ideas to a group.
leelaQ: Where do you suggest for a family dinner?
answer: How about trying the new restaurant near our house?

en: It's too noisy to study here.
context: Complaining about a noisy place.
explain: 'Too + adjective + to + verb' shows something is more than you can accept.
usage: Use it to explain why a place does not suit you.
leelaQ: Where is it too noisy for you to study?
answer: It is too noisy near the main road.

en: The soup is not hot enough.
context: Telling a waiter politely.
explain: 'Enough' comes after the adjective: 'hot enough'.
usage: Use it politely at a restaurant when food is not right.
leelaQ: How do you tell a waiter that the food is cold?
answer: I say, the soup is not hot enough, please change it.

en: He drives carefully on the highway.
context: Telling someone about a safe driver.
explain: Add -ly to many adjectives to make adverbs, such as careful to carefully.
usage: Use it to describe how someone does something.
leelaQ: How do you drive or walk on a busy road?
answer: I walk carefully and look at both sides.

en: Would you pass me the salt, please?
context: Asking someone at the dinner table.
explain: 'Would you' + please is a polite request.
usage: Use it at the table with family or guests.
leelaQ: What do you ask for at the dinner table?
answer: I ask, would you pass me the water, please?

en: Please don't park your bike in front of the gate.
tamil: தயவு செய்து கேட்டுக்கு முன்னாடி பைக்கை நிறுத்தாதீங்க.
context: Asking a neighbour politely.
explain: 'Please don't' + verb is a polite negative request.
usage: Use it with neighbours to correct something politely.
leelaQ: How do you ask a neighbour not to make noise?
answer: I say, please don't play loud music at night.

en: I wish I could speak English more confidently.
tamil: நான் இன்னும் தன்னம்பிக்கையா ஆங்கிலம் பேச முடிஞ்சா நல்லா இருக்கும்.
context: Sharing a learning goal with a friend.
explain: 'I wish' + could/past form expresses a wish about the present.
usage: Use it when you talk about something you want to change.
leelaQ: What do you wish you could do better in English?
answer: I wish I could speak with more confidence.

en: If you had told me, I would have helped you.
context: Gently telling a friend you could have helped.
explain: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle, for an unreal past.
usage: Use it when you talk about what could have happened in the past.
leelaQ: What would you have done differently last year?
answer: I would have studied more if I had known.

en: By next year, I will have finished my degree.
tamil: அடுத்த வருஷம் நான் என் டிகிரியை முடிச்சிருப்பேன்.
context: Sharing your future goal in an interview.
explain: Future perfect (will have + past participle) shows something will be complete by a future time.
usage: Use it to describe a goal you will complete by a certain time.
leelaQ: What will you have achieved by next year?
answer: I will have learned to speak English fluently.

en: This time tomorrow, I will be travelling to Delhi.
tamil: நாளைக்கு இந்த நேரம் நான் டெல்லிக்கு பயணம் பண்ணிட்டு இருப்பேன்.
context: Telling a colleague your travel plans.
explain: Future continuous (will be + verb-ing) shows an action that will be in progress at a future time.
usage: Use it to explain where you will be at a certain time.
leelaQ: Where will you be this time next week?
answer: I will be sitting in my office this time next week.

en: Not only is he smart, but he is also kind.
context: Praising a friend to others.
explain: 'Not only ... but also' joins two good points; the word order flips after 'Not only'.
usage: Use it when you speak highly of someone.
leelaQ: Who is a person you admire, and why?
answer: My teacher is not only strict, but also very kind.

en: Speaking in English every day makes you more confident.
tamil: தினமும் ஆங்கிலத்துல பேசறது உன்ன இன்னும் தன்னம்பிக்கை ஆக்கும்.
context: Motivating a classmate.
explain: A verb-ing phrase (a gerund) can be the subject of a sentence.
usage: Use it when you give advice about learning habits.
leelaQ: What helps you feel confident when you speak?
answer: Speaking slowly and clearly helps me feel confident.

en: I'm waiting for the bus, so I'll text you later.
tamil: நான் பஸ்ஸுக்கு காத்துட்டு இருக்கேன், அதனால அப்புறம் மெசேஜ் பண்றேன்.
context: Replying to a friend's call while outside.
explain: 'So' joins a reason with a result. Present continuous shows what is happening now.
usage: Use it when you cannot talk because you are busy.
leelaQ: What are you waiting for these days?
answer: I am waiting for my exam results.

en: Hurry up, we're running out of time.
context: Telling a friend before an exam or a train.
explain: 'Run out of' means to have no more of something; the imperative 'Hurry up' urges quick action.
usage: Use it with friends or family when time is short.
leelaQ: What do you say when you are running late?
answer: I say, hurry up, we are running late.

en: Wait here, I'll get the car.
tamil: இங்கயே இரு, நான் காரை எடுத்துட்டு வரேன்.
context: Telling an elderly relative at the hospital.
explain: 'Wait here' is a direct instruction; 'I'll' adds a quick decision.
usage: Use it when you ask someone to stay while you do something.
leelaQ: What do you tell your parents when you go to get something?
answer: I tell them to sit here while I bring it.

en: Do you want me to help you with the luggage?
context: Offering help at the railway station.
explain: 'Do you want me to' + verb is a natural way to offer help.
usage: Use it to offer help to a friend or traveller.
leelaQ: How do you offer help to a friend who is moving house?
answer: I say, do you want me to carry some boxes?

en: Are you free this Saturday afternoon?
context: Inviting a friend for lunch.
explain: 'Are you free' is a simple way to ask if someone is available.
usage: Use it to invite a friend or colleague.
leelaQ: What do you do when you are free on Saturdays?
answer: I meet my friends and play cricket.

en: Whose bag is this on the chair?
context: Finding the owner of a lost bag.
explain: 'Whose' asks about the owner of something.
usage: Use it in a class or office when you find something left behind.
leelaQ: What do you ask if you find a wallet on the road?
answer: I ask, whose wallet is this?

en: The movie had already started when we got there.
tamil: நாங்க அங்க போனப்போ படம் ஏற்கனவே ஆரம்பிச்சிருச்சு.
context: Telling a friend about a missed start.
explain: Past perfect shows the earlier event ('had started') before 'got there'.
usage: Use it to explain why you missed something.
leelaQ: Have you ever reached a movie late? What happened?
answer: Yes, the movie had started and we missed the first scene.

en: It's the first time I have flown in an aeroplane.
tamil: நான் விமானத்துல பறக்கறது இதுதான் முதல் தடவை.
context: Sharing your excitement with a co-passenger.
explain: 'It's the first time' is followed by present perfect.
usage: Use it to share a new experience with others.
leelaQ: What is a first-time experience you remember?
answer: It was my first time riding a metro train.

en: I've been learning English for six months.
tamil: நான் ஆறு மாசமா ஆங்கிலம் கத்துக்கிட்டு இருக்கேன்.
context: Introducing yourself in a language class.
explain: Present perfect continuous with 'for' shows how long an action has been going on.
usage: Use it to tell someone about your learning journey.
leelaQ: How long have you been learning English?
answer: I have been learning English for one year.

en: I haven't seen him since last year.
tamil: நான் அவனை போன வருஷத்துல இருந்து பாக்கல.
context: Talking about an old friend.
explain: 'Since' + a point in time is used with present perfect to show the start of a period.
usage: Use it when you talk about a person or place you have not met for a long time.
leelaQ: Who haven't you met for a long time?
answer: I haven't met my school friends for five years.

en: Let me know if you need anything.
context: Offering help to a new colleague.
explain: 'Let me know' + if-clause is a friendly way to offer help.
usage: Use it at work or home to show you are ready to help.
leelaQ: What do you say to a friend who is moving to a new place?
answer: I say, let me know if you need any help.

en: Take your time, there is no hurry.
context: Reassuring a nervous colleague.
explain: 'Take your time' is a kind phrase that tells someone not to rush.
usage: Use it when someone feels pressure and needs reassurance.
leelaQ: What do you say to a friend who is nervous?
answer: I say, take your time, there is no hurry.

en: Give me a call when you reach home.
tamil: வீட்டுக்கு போனதும் எனக்கு ஒரு கால் பண்ணு.
context: Saying goodbye to a friend at night.
explain: 'Give me a call' is an informal imperative meaning to phone me.
usage: Use it with friends or family when you care about their safe arrival.
leelaQ: What do you tell a friend who is travelling alone?
answer: I tell him to call me when he reaches home.

en: Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.
tamil: தயவு செய்து உட்காருங்க, சங்கோஜம் இல்லாம இருங்க.
context: Welcoming a guest into your home.
explain: Two imperatives joined by 'and' give a warm welcome.
usage: Use it when you welcome guests to your home.
leelaQ: What do you say when a guest arrives at your home?
answer: I say, please sit down and have some water.

en: Mind the gap while stepping into the train.
context: Warning a child at the metro station.
explain: 'Mind' + noun is an imperative that means 'be careful of'.
usage: Use it for a safety warning in public places.
leelaQ: What safety warnings do you know from public places?
answer: I know 'mind the step' and 'wet floor'.

en: He neither called nor sent a message.
tamil: அவன் கால் பண்ணவும் இல்ல, மெசேஜ் அனுப்பவும் இல்ல.
context: Complaining about a friend's silence.
explain: 'Neither ... nor' joins two negative ideas; the verb itself stays in positive form.
usage: Use it when you complain gently about someone who did nothing.
leelaQ: Has someone ever forgotten to call you? What happened?
answer: My friend neither called nor texted on my birthday.

en: Make sure you lock the door.
context: Reminding a family member leaving home.
explain: 'Make sure' + clause tells someone to be certain something is done.
usage: Use it with family or roommates before leaving home.
leelaQ: What do you make sure of before you sleep?
answer: I make sure the doors are locked and the gas is off.

en: Where did you buy that lovely saree?
context: Asking a relative at a function.
explain: Past simple question: where + did + subject + base verb.
usage: Use it to start a friendly chat about clothes or shopping.
leelaQ: Where did you buy your favourite shirt?
answer: I bought it at a small shop near my house.

en: Who is going to cook tonight?
context: Asking family members at home.
explain: 'Who is going to' asks about a plan or intention.
usage: Use it at home when you share household work.
leelaQ: Who cooks in your house on Sundays?
answer: My father cooks on Sundays, and he makes biryani.

en: What did the doctor say about your knee?
tamil: உன் முழங்கால் பத்தி டாக்டர் என்ன சொன்னார்?
context: Asking a relative who visited a hospital.
explain: 'What did ... say' is a past simple question about a conversation.
usage: Use it to ask about someone's health with care.
leelaQ: What did your doctor say the last time you visited?
answer: He said I should rest and drink more water.

en: Is there a pharmacy near here?
context: Asking a stranger in an unknown area.
explain: 'Is there' asks if something exists in a place.
usage: Use it when you travel and need a shop quickly.
leelaQ: What do you ask when you are in a new town?
answer: I ask, is there a good restaurant near here?
